opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it was honestly a bit of a strange feeling, in a good way. When you leave, you think you remember everything, but you forget how much of your day-to-day was shaped by the tooling. Coming back felt a little like returning to your old hometown: the streets are mostly where you left them, but some new buildings have gone up, some shops have closed, and you have to relearn a few shortcuts.

The thing that hit me most was how *smooth* it is when you're working at scale. When I was outside, at a startup, we were constantly fighting the infrastructure: debugging cluster issues, dealing with flaky nodes, figuring out why a run diverged, and whether it was the model or the hardware. A huge fraction of your mental energy goes to keeping things alive. Back at Google, the TPU stack and all the internal tooling just absorb so much of that pain. You can spend your time thinking about the actual research question rather than babysitting jobs. That's an enormous productivity multiplier that's easy to take for granted until you've lived without it.

At the same time, there was definitely a ramp-up. Codebases evolve, things get renamed, the way teams are organized shifts. So the first few weeks were me re-onboarding, asking slightly embarrassing questions, and reading a lot of docs. But the muscle memory came back pretty quickly.

I'd also say being away gave me a different appreciation for it. At a startup you learn to be very scrappy and very opinionated about what actually matters, because you can't afford to waste compute or time. Bringing that mindset back into a place with this much infrastructure is, I think, a really nice combination. You have the scrappiness and the urgency, and now you also have the rocket ship underneath you. So overall it felt a bit like coming home, but coming home as a slightly different person.

r001.rationale: The response compares returning to Google to coming back to an old hometown, not to resuming a saved video game.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so it's funny, because the first thing I felt coming back was just how much I'd missed the infrastructure. Like, I didn't fully appreciate it until I was outside. When I was at Reka, we were building everything from scratch, dealing with GPUs, dealing with different cloud providers, nodes going down, all of that. And it's not that it's bad, it's just that you spend a lot of your cycles on things that aren't really the research.

So coming back to DeepMind, having TPUs and the whole stack where you can just, you know, write your model and it kind of runs at scale, that's a huge quality-of-life thing. The compiler, the tooling, the way the pods are set up, it's all very mature. You take it for granted when you're inside, and then you leave and realize, oh, this is actually kind of a privilege.

But I'd also say I came back as a different person. Being on the outside taught me a lot about what actually matters when you have constraints. Like, at Google you can sometimes be a bit wasteful because compute is abundant, and you don't think too hard about efficiency. At a startup, every run has to count, you're much more careful about what experiments you launch. So I think I came back with a bit more of that discipline, and also a lot more appreciation for the people who built and maintain the infra, because I'd seen what it takes to try to replicate even a fraction of that.

The other thing is the org had changed quite a bit. Brain and DeepMind had merged while I was away, so it wasn't exactly the same place I left. Some of the tools were different, some of the codebases had moved on, a lot of people I used to work with had shuffled around. So there was a bit of relearning. But the core of it, the TPU stack, the research culture, that part felt very familiar. It was kind of like coming home, but the furniture had been rearranged.

r001.rationale: The response describes returning as “kind of like coming home,” but does not compare it to resuming a saved video game.

astra-6.text: Coming back, I had a different appreciation for the infrastructure. When you’ve been working within a system, you get used to it—you don’t necessarily notice everything it’s doing for you. After spending time away, you come back and see how much work goes into making research at that scale possible. There’s still the adjustment of getting familiar with things again, but there’s also that feeling of, okay, I can focus on the experiments, and there’s a lot here to support that.
